result: The manuscript establishes the context and motivation for developing chicken germplasm cryopreservation technology by describing the global chicken population, the diversity and importance of local breeds, the threats to these breeds from commercial farming practices, and the value of chickens as research models.
evaluation: Claims C1-C8 are all supported by appropriate citations to prior literature (Ritchie and Roser 2021, DAD-IS 2021, Alders and Pym 2019, Melesse 2019, Davey et al. 2018, Fulton and Delany 2003). These claims provide well-established background information that contextualizes the need for the technology developed in this study.

result: The manuscript reviews the limitations of current avian gamete cryopreservation methods, noting that while cryopreservation is routine in ruminants, avian eggs cannot be cryopreserved and chicken semen cryopreservation has poor fertilization rates due to multiple biological and technical factors.
evaluation: Claims C9-C15 are supported by citations to established literature (Blesbois et al. 2007, 2008; Thélie et al. 2019; Matsuzaki et al. 2021) and represent well-accepted knowledge in the field. The mechanistic explanations for poor semen cryopreservation outcomes (C15) are appropriately presented as hypotheses supported by citations.

result: The manuscript reviews prior work on avian primordial germ cell (PGC) biology and cryopreservation, including PGC migration and development, in vitro culture methods, and the use of genetically modified surrogate hosts (DDX4 and iCaspase9 lines) to generate offspring from cryopreserved PGCs.
evaluation: Claims C16-C27 are well-supported by citations to prior literature (Karagenç et al. 1996, Tsunekawa et al. 2000, Lee et al. 2016, van de Lavoir et al. 2006, Whyte et al. 2015, Nakamura et al. 2008, Macdonald et al. 2010, Woodcock et al. 2019, Ballantyne et al. 2021a, 2021b). These claims accurately represent established knowledge and prior work that forms the foundation for the current study.

result: The manuscript identifies limitations of in vitro PGC propagation, noting it is technically demanding, expensive, requires specialized facilities, and leads to epigenetic modifications and reduced germline transmission with extended culture.
evaluation: Claims C28-C29 are supported by citations (Woodcock et al. 2019, Ballantyne et al. 2021a, Soler et al. 2021) and represent established knowledge about the challenges of PGC culture. These limitations provide the rationale for developing the direct gonadal cryopreservation method presented in this study.

result: The manuscript reviews the developmental biology of avian gonadal germ cells, including their proliferation during embryonic development, sex-specific developmental trajectories, and the demonstrated ability of gonadal germ cells to remigrate and colonize host gonads to produce functional gametes and offspring.
evaluation: Claims C30-C34 are supported by appropriate citations (Hughes 1963, Tajima et al. 1998, Naito et al. 2007, Mozdziak et al. 2006). These claims establish the biological foundation for the direct gonadal cryopreservation approach by demonstrating that gonadal germ cells retain the capacity to colonize host embryos and produce offspring.

result: The manuscript quantifies the germ cell population in chicken gonads between ED 9-12, demonstrating that female gonads contain over 10,000 germ cells by ED 10 (increasing from 1.9% to 10.6% of total cells) and male gonads also exceed 10,000 germ cells by ED 10 (maintaining 2.4-2.9% of total cells), with gonadal cells up to ED 10 capable of efficient re-migration.
evaluation: Claims C35-C36 and C44-C50 are supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2A using fluorescently labeled iCaspase9 reporter chickens. The quantification appears methodologically sound with appropriate sample sizes (n=3-7 gonad pairs per timepoint). The conclusion that gonads contain >10,000 germ cells by ED 10 is a reasonable inference from the data showing total cell numbers and germ cell percentages.

result: The manuscript demonstrates that cryopreservation of whole gonads followed by thawing and dissociation maintains significantly better cell viability compared to cryopreservation of dissociated gonadal cells, with the authors speculating this may be due to adverse effects of enzymatic dissociation on cryopreservation.
evaluation: Claims C51-C52 and C100-C101 are supported by experimental data in Figure 2B showing viability comparisons between fresh cells, frozen dissociated cells, and frozen whole gonads. The statistical significance is stated but p-values are not provided in the figure. The mechanistic explanation (C101) is appropriately presented as speculation. This is a key technical finding that justifies the whole-gonad cryopreservation approach.

result: The manuscript demonstrates that gonadal cells from ED 8-10 donor embryos achieve repeatable colonization of host gonads, while ED 11 donor cells result in much fewer fluorescent cells in host embryos.
evaluation: Claims C53-C54 are supported by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 showing colonization results from different embryonic stages. The data support the conclusion that ED 8-10 is the optimal window for gonadal cell collection, which is critical for the practical application of this technology.

result: The manuscript demonstrates that SSEA-1 antibody-based MACS enrichment of female gonadal cells achieves >40-fold enrichment of germ cells (from 1.17% to 46%), with 94% viability and co-expression of SSEA-1, yielding approximately 5000 germ cells per pair of ED 9 female gonads, with SSEA-1 expression decreasing after ED 10.
evaluation: Claims C55-C63 are supported by experimental data in Figures 2C, 2D, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2, along with appropriate citations (Hughes 1963, Urven et al. 1988, Kim et al. 2004, Mozdziak et al. 2005, 2006). The MACS enrichment data are clearly presented with flow cytometry analysis. This technical development is important for achieving sufficient female germ cell numbers for successful colonization.

result: The manuscript demonstrates that cryopreserved gonadal cells (both male and female) successfully colonize sex-matched iCaspase9 host embryo gonads, with the majority of cells being GFP+ and fewer RFP+ cells present, and that these cells persist and differentiate in adult testes.
evaluation: Claims C64-C66 are supported by experimental data in Figures 2E and 2F showing colonization of ED 14 host gonads and adult testes. The fluorescent imaging clearly demonstrates colonization by donor cells. This is a critical proof-of-concept result showing that the cryopreserved gonadal cells retain functionality.

result: The manuscript describes the methodology for visual sexing, pooling, and cryopreservation of ED 9 gonads, followed by thawing, dissociation, and injection into iCaspase9 or DDX4 host embryos, achieving hatchability rates of 40-83% and estimating that 6 ED 10 embryos can generate 10 host chicks.
evaluation: Claims C37-C41 and C67-C71 are supported by experimental data in Table 1 and detailed methodology descriptions. The hatchability improvement from 40% to 58-83% after modifying incubation conditions demonstrates experimental optimization. The genetic predictions for iCaspase9 (100% heterozygotes) and DDX4 (25% correct genotype) are based on sound genetic principles. These claims establish the practical feasibility of the method.

result: The manuscript demonstrates that male iCaspase9 surrogate hosts injected with cryopreserved male gonadal cells achieve high fertility (83-99%), transmit multiple donor genotypes (both GFP+ and RFP+ offspring), with 6 of 7 males producing exclusively donor-derived offspring and 1 of 7 males producing 88% donor-derived and 12% host-derived offspring.
evaluation: Claims C72-C75 are supported by experimental data in Table 2 and Figure 3A. The fertility rates are clearly documented, and the detection of both GFP+ and RFP+ embryos demonstrates transmission of multiple genotypes. The calculation that 12% of embryos derive from endogenous germ cells (based on 6% transgene transmission in heterozygotes) is mathematically sound. This demonstrates successful germline transmission through male hosts.

result: The manuscript demonstrates that female iCaspase9 surrogate hosts injected with cryopreserved female gonadal cells lay 5.0-6.3 eggs per week (comparable to wildtype controls at 4.1-6.9 eggs/week), achieve 80-98% fertility, transmit multiple donor genotypes (both GFP+ and RFP+ offspring), with all 12 iCaspase9 females producing exclusively donor-derived offspring (634 embryos total).
evaluation: Claims C76-C80 are supported by experimental data in Table 3 and Figure 4A. The laying rates demonstrate that surrogate hosts maintain normal reproductive function. The absence of transgene transmission in all 12 females (0/634 embryos) indicates complete sterilization and exclusive donor-derived offspring. This demonstrates successful germline transmission through female hosts with high efficiency.

result: The manuscript demonstrates that Sire Dam Surrogate (SDS) mating of male and female iCaspase9 hosts carrying cryopreserved gonadal cells produces offspring with 90-99% fertility and 91% hatchability, including 'yellow' (RFP+GFP+) offspring derived entirely from cryopreserved donor male and female germ cells.
evaluation: Claims C81-C82, C43, and C115 are supported by experimental data in Table 4 and Figure 5. The presence of yellow (double-positive) offspring provides direct evidence that both male and female gametes derived from cryopreserved gonadal cells can combine to produce viable offspring. This is the key demonstration that the technology can regenerate a breed without any genetic contribution from surrogate hosts.

result: The manuscript demonstrates that gonadal germ cells can form functional gametes in opposite-sex hosts: female gonadal cells injected into male iCaspase9 hosts produce functional spermatozoa achieving >95% fertilization and GFP+ offspring, while male gonadal cells injected into female hosts produce mature follicles, though with unusual testicular morphology and absence of RFP+ transmission in the female-to-male direction.
evaluation: Claims C83-C89 and C102-C104 are partially supported by experimental data in Table 5 and Figures 3B, 4B. The demonstration of female cells producing functional sperm in male hosts is well-supported (>95% fertility, GFP+ offspring). However, the absence of RFP+ embryos (C87) is unexplained and contradicts expectations. The unusual testicular morphology (C88) suggests incomplete or abnormal gametogenesis. The prior work cited (C102-C104, Ballantyne et al. 2021a) used in vitro cultured PGCs, which may behave differently than gonadal cells. More investigation is needed to understand why RFP transmission failed and whether this represents a technical issue or biological limitation.

result: The manuscript demonstrates that individual male surrogate hosts transmit donor genotypes at varying frequencies (ranging from 3-28% for RFP+ in CRYO-1M and 5-21% in CRYO-4M), with individual males often differing significantly from expected transmission rates, but cohorts of males collectively transmitting genotypes proportionally to input ratios (14% vs. 11.1% expected for CRYO-1M, 11% vs. 11.1% expected for CRYO-4M).
evaluation: Claims C90-C95 are supported by experimental data and statistical analysis in Table 6. The statistical testing appropriately uses exact proportion tests to compare observed vs. expected transmission rates. The finding that individual males vary but cohorts maintain expected ratios is biologically plausible and important for practical application. The data suggest that using multiple surrogate males ensures representation of all donor genotypes.

result: The manuscript demonstrates that female surrogate host cohorts show significant deviations from expected genotype transmission rates (14% vs. 19.0% expected for CRYO-2F, 24% vs. 17.4% expected for CRYO-3F, 20% vs. 11.1% expected for DDX4 females), suggesting that different donor genotypes transmit with different efficiencies, possibly due to competition in the gonadal niche.
evaluation: Claims C96-C99 and C105 are supported by experimental data and statistical analysis in Table 6. The significant deviations from expected transmission rates in female cohorts contrast with the male results where cohorts maintained expected ratios. The interpretation that genotypes may compete differently in the gonadal niche (C105) is reasonable speculation based on the data. However, the female cohorts were housed collectively, which prevents individual-level analysis and may introduce confounding factors.

result: The manuscript demonstrates that the iCaspase9 line is superior to the DDX4 line for generating sex-matched chimeras, producing 100% suitable host embryos compared to 25% for DDX4, though with the tradeoff that poorly injected iCaspase9 hosts can transmit endogenous transgenes (observed in 1 of 7 males and 0 of 12 females).
evaluation: Claims C106-C109 are supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript and citations to prior work (Taylor et al. 2017, Woodcock et al. 2019). The genetic comparison is sound: iCaspase9 homozygous males × wildtype females produce 100% heterozygous embryos suitable as hosts, while DDX4 heterozygous males × wildtype females produce only 25% suitable Z-W females. The observation of incomplete sterilization in 1 of 7 males is an important limitation that should be addressed in future work.

result: The manuscript demonstrates that the technology can meet FAO guidelines for breed conservation, which recommend 13 unrelated males and 13 unrelated females to maintain <1% inbreeding, by showing that surrogate hosts carrying 12 male and 14 female donor genotypes can theoretically regenerate a genetically diverse population.
evaluation: Claims C110-C111 are supported by citation to FAO guidelines (Food and Agriculture Organization 1998) and inference from the experimental data showing transmission of multiple genotypes. The calculation that 12 male and 14 female genotypes meet the FAO threshold is reasonable, though the actual inbreeding coefficient would depend on the relatedness of the donor individuals, which is not discussed. This demonstrates the practical utility of the technology for conservation purposes.

result: The manuscript asserts that genome editing and iCaspase9-induced apoptosis have minimal welfare impact on surrogate hosts compared to chemical and physical sterility treatments, which have high impact on host health.
evaluation: Claims C112-C113 are presented as general knowledge without supporting citations or data. While the assertion is plausible, no welfare assessment data are provided in this manuscript. The surrogate hosts appear to have normal reproductive function (laying rates, fertility), which supports the claim of minimal impact, but formal welfare evaluation would strengthen this conclusion. This is an important ethical consideration for the technology.

result: The manuscript concludes that this low-tech, cost-effective technology is particularly suited for conserving the >1600 chicken breeds raised in low and lower-middle income countries under resource-limited conditions and will enable conservation efforts for both commercial and smallholder farmers.
evaluation: Claim C114 is presented as general knowledge without citation, though the statement about breed distribution is plausible. Claim C116 is speculative about future applications. While the technology is simpler than in vitro PGC culture, it still requires: (1) access to transgenic surrogate host lines, (2) embryo injection capabilities, (3) liquid nitrogen storage, (4) MACS equipment for female cells. The feasibility in resource-limited settings is not demonstrated and would require additional validation. The technology's utility for conservation is promising but requires further development for LMIC contexts.
